claims.text: Premelting and melting progression in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are primarily governed by Cu surface segregation.
Cu has a lower intrinsic melting point than the other principal constituents of FeNiCrCoCu.
Initially solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are compositionally homogeneous.
During heating, Cu atoms tend to migrate to the nanoparticle surface.
Heating produces a Cu-rich surface layer and surface compositional gradient.
The Cu-rich surface layer acts as a nucleation site for the phase transition.
Cu enrichment lowers the local melting temperature at the nanoparticle surface.
Melting initiates at the Cu-enriched nanoparticle surface.
The melted region progressively propagates from the nanoparticle surface toward the core.
Nanoparticles with substantial Cu surface segregation will have a lower melting-onset temperature than nanoparticles in which segregation is inhibited.
Nanoparticles with substantial Cu surface segregation will show more distinct surface-to-core melting than nanoparticles in which segregation is inhibited.
A conformal inert oxide or carbon coating can inhibit Cu surface segregation.
An inert atmosphere prevents oxidation during heating.
Surface effects dominate the relevant thermal behavior for FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles approximately 10–50 nm in size.
Particle-size variation or external contaminants can alter nanoparticle melting behavior.
Surface-energy effects and nanoparticle morphology may also influence melting.
The proposed comparison uses coated and untreated nanoparticles from the same synthesis batch under otherwise similar heating conditions.
Failure of confirmed segregation inhibition to raise melting onset or alter melting progression would falsify the proposed governing role of Cu segregation.
